opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say it's fundamentally the wrong direction. I just think we're still at a stage where we don't fully understand the paradigm in the settings where it's easiest to study, which is mostly language modeling and sequence modeling more broadly.

Nested Learning is a way of looking at a model as a set of nested optimization problems, each running at its own update frequency. Some components change very quickly, almost like working memory. Others change slowly and hold more persistent knowledge. Once you see things that way, architectures like Transformers, the optimizers we train them with, and even ideas like continual learning start to look like different levels of the same system. That's exciting, but there's a lot we still don't know. How many levels do you actually need? How should the frequencies be chosen? How does knowledge move between levels without catastrophic forgetting? What are the right inductive biases for each level? We're still working these out, even in language, where we have good benchmarks, a lot of data, and a fairly clear sense of what success looks like.

Robotics and world modeling add a lot of extra complexity. The data is far more expensive and much noisier. You're dealing with continuous, high-dimensional, multimodal inputs, and you have embodiment and real-time constraints. Evaluation is also much harder. If you take a paradigm you don't fully understand and drop it into that environment, it becomes very difficult to attribute what's happening. When something works or fails, is it because of the multi-timescale memory design, or because of the data, the simulator, the control stack, or one of a dozen other factors? You lose the ability to do clean science.

Ironically, I think robotics may eventually be one of the most natural fits for these ideas. A robot really does need to adapt at test time, keep learning continually, and remember things across very different time horizons, from the last few milliseconds of sensor data to skills learned over months. That's exactly what this framework is trying to capture. So I see it as a sequencing question. First we need to really understand the building blocks in more controlled settings, things like the self-modifying components and the continuum memory systems, and get them to scale reliably. Once that foundation is solid, moving into world models and robotics will be much more meaningful, and I expect we'll see people doing exactly that.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes understanding Nested Learning in controlled settings before applying it to world modeling. It notes world modeling’s added complexity, but does not say that addressing foundational challenges in world modeling takes priority over applying Nested Learning there.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the main reason is that we don't yet fully understand the thing we built, even in the setting where it's easiest to study.

Nested Learning, at its core, is a way of looking at a model as a set of optimization problems running at different frequencies, with different levels of memory. Some components update every token, some update every few hundred tokens, some are effectively frozen. In language modeling, that structure is relatively clean. The data is a one-dimensional stream of discrete tokens, we have very strong baselines, and we have decades of intuition about what "in-context learning" means and how to measure it. So when we see the continual-memory system doing something interesting, we can actually attribute it. We can ask, is this gain coming from the fast memory, from the slow memory, from the way the optimizer itself is being treated as a learned module? We have the tools to isolate that.

Robotics and world modeling throw away almost all of those advantages at once. The inputs are continuous, high-dimensional, multimodal. The time scales are not given to you by a tokenizer; they're given to you by physics and by the task, and they vary enormously. A grasp happens in milliseconds, learning the layout of a kitchen happens over minutes or hours, and the dynamics of the world are something you'd want to keep for the lifetime of the system. In principle that's exactly the kind of multi-frequency structure Nested Learning is meant to express. But that's the problem. It fits the story so well that it's tempting to just go and claim it, and I don't think we've earned that yet.

There are concrete open questions. One is what the "levels" should even be in that setting, and whether they should be chosen by hand or discovered. Another is stability. In language we can get away with a fast memory that occasionally makes a bad update, because the next token corrects it. In a control loop, a bad fast update can put the robot in a state you can't recover from, and the model never sees the data that would have fixed it. The continual learning that we're excited about becomes a safety liability if you don't understand how errors propagate across levels. And the third is just evaluation. We don't have a good benchmark that cleanly tests whether a world model is learning at the right time scale versus just memorizing recent frames.

So my view is that the right order of operations is to push harder on the places where we can still measure things precisely. Longer contexts, harder continual-learning setups, understanding what the different memory levels are actually storing. Once we have a real theory of why the hierarchy helps, rather than a nice picture that it helps, then moving to embodied settings becomes a translation problem instead of a guess. I'd rather be a year late and know why it works than be first and not be able to explain a failure.

r001.rationale: The response identifies unresolved world-modeling issues—how to define memory levels, stability and error propagation, and evaluation—and argues that the foundations should be understood before moving Nested Learning into embodied settings.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s too early mainly because we still need to understand what Nested Learning buys us in simpler, more controlled settings. The motivation is relevant to robotics: you want a system that can keep learning from experience, adapt quickly to changes, and retain knowledge over longer timescales. But that motivation is not yet evidence that it will work well in a robot.

With robotics and world modeling, you’re adding several difficult problems at once. What should the system learn online? What should remain stable? What feedback tells it that an update was useful? And how do errors in its predictions affect the actions it takes and, therefore, the data it sees next?

So I wouldn’t say we should avoid those applications. I’d say we need to establish the learning mechanisms first—show that the different levels actually learn and retain the right things—before making strong claims about world models or embodied intelligence.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to establish Nested Learning’s mechanisms in simpler settings before making strong claims about world models, but it does not identify foundational challenges in world modeling as a higher priority.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s too early in the sense that we still need to understand and validate the basic ideas, not that robotics or world modeling are somehow outside the scope of Nested Learning. Those are actually very natural settings for it: you have information changing at different timescales, and the system needs to keep learning without overwriting everything it already knows.

But robotics introduces a lot of additional complexity. If something fails, is it because of the learning algorithm, the perception system, the data, or the interaction with the environment? It becomes harder to isolate what the framework is actually contributing. And with world modeling, we still have to establish how these different levels of learning should interact to produce useful predictions over time.

So I would start with more controlled settings, understand when the approach works and where it breaks, and then move toward those applications. I’m excited about that direction; I just think we need a stronger experimental foundation before making big claims.

r001.rationale: The response says world modeling still needs work to establish how its learning levels interact, and recommends building a stronger experimental foundation before moving toward these applications.
